 EPFO eases withdrawal rules, opens door to systematic payouts for retirees 
 EPFO has approved a major overhaul of provident fund withdrawal rules, including a systematic withdrawal plan for retirees and easier access for partial withdrawals. The board also cleared new contribution channels and wider investment options, signalling a push to make retirement savings more flexible and more inclusive. ETRajasthan

 Retirement savings held with the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation are set for a major reset, with the fund body moving to make withdrawals more flexible while also trying to preserve long-term income for members. The latest decisions could change how millions of workers treat provident fund balances at the point of retirement and during periods of financial need. First reported by Times of India . In a set of reforms approved by the Central Board of Trustees , EPFO has said retiring members will be able to opt for a systematic withdrawal plan, or SWP, instead of being forced to take out their entire corpus within a short window after retirement. The change is designed to let members keep part of their savings invested and continue earning interest on the balance. Retirees can now spread withdrawals over time Under the new framework, a member reaching retirement can choose to withdraw provident fund savings in instalments at intervals that suit personal cash-flow needs. The payout cycle may be monthly, quarterly or half-yearly, depending on the subscriber's preference. Members will also be able to stop the SWP whenever they wish, or combine it with partial lump-sum withdrawals and interest-only withdrawals. The retirement fund body said the voluntary structure is meant to create a more stable post-retirement income stream and reduce the risk that retirees exhaust their savings too quickly. It also argued that the design should lower reinvestment risk, since members will not need to move large sums into other products immediately after retirement. Until now, retiring members were required to withdraw the full corpus within three years. The new option marks a significant shift in how provident fund money can be accessed after a working life of compulsory contributions. Partial withdrawals become easier for members in need The board has also relaxed rules for partial withdrawals. After requiring members for about a year to maintain a minimum balance of 25 per cent in their account, EPFO has now allowed up to 90 per cent withdrawal of the corpus for three specified purposes: essential needs such as illness, education and marriage; housing requirements; and special circumstances. At the same time, the waiting period for withdrawals linked to joblessness has been reduced sharply to two months from 12 months earlier. The organisation said the revised provisions were approved with an eye on protecting the long-term social security interests of EPF members while still giving them more room to manage emergencies. The minimum waiting period under the Employees' Pension Scheme remains unchanged at 36 months, keeping a separate check on pension-related withdrawals even as provident fund access becomes easier in other categories. Who stands to gain from the new system According to the retirement fund body, around 6.3 lakh EPF members aged above 55 years and holding provident fund accumulations of more than ₹5 lakh are expected to be the main beneficiaries of the SWP structure. For this group, the ability to draw down savings in stages could provide a smoother transition from salary income to retirement income. The rules also provide for continuity in the event of a member's death during the payout period. In that case, a nominee or dependant will be able either to withdraw the remaining balance or continue receiving periodic payments, depending on the structure chosen earlier. TOI reported about the proposed changes in a front-page report on Thursday, highlighting the scale of the shift in withdrawal norms and the wider implications for retirement planning among salaried workers. Supporters see a safer alternative to lump sums Vineet Nahata , managing director at Power Gilt Treasuries and a member of the Central Board of Trustees, said the revised framework gives members a fixed-income avenue with tax efficiency and better visibility over post-retirement cash flows. He said the structure can be more dependable than bank fixed deposits and mutual funds, which are exposed to credit risk and market volatility. His comments reflect a broader policy intent behind the move: to encourage provident fund members to treat retirement savings as a long-term income source rather than a one-time payout. For many households, especially those with limited financial buffers, the challenge after retirement is not just preserving capital but ensuring that money lasts through a longer lifespan. EPFO widens the funding and investment canvas The board did not stop at withdrawal rules. In another major move aimed at broadening social security coverage, it approved a UAN-linked mechanism that will allow direct voluntary contributions and third-party micro-contributions, including customer tips, without depending on the traditional employer payroll channel. That change is intended to help workers in the unorganised sector build provident fund savings on their own, even if they do not have a formal employer contribution structure. If implemented smoothly, the mechanism could become a useful bridge between informal earnings and formal retirement savings, expanding the reach of EPFO beyond its traditional salaried base. The organisation also decided to diversify its investment portfolio by allowing up to 3 per cent of fresh annual accretions to be invested in eligible alternative investment funds. In addition, it may deploy up to 5 per cent of fresh annual accretions in asset-backed and trust-structured investments, in line with its investment pattern. Initially, the plan is to route worker capital through institutional platforms such as the National Investment and Infrastructure Fund and Sidbi's Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0 . The broader goal is to seek higher returns for EPFO's 30 crore members while keeping the portfolio aligned with approved investment norms. Exempted trusts could move back under direct EPFO control Another part of the board's agenda dealt with exempted establishments, where employers manage provident fund accounts on their own under EPFO rules. The board reviewed proposals from 27 establishments seeking to surrender their exemption status and four more asking for cancellation of exemption, a shift that would bring roughly ₹6,000 crore of corpus and about 1.5 lakh members under direct EPFO administration. For members, such a transfer can mean a more standardised administrative structure and closer oversight by the central retirement fund system. For EPFO, it adds to the pool of directly managed assets and strengthens its role as the primary custodian of formal retirement savings. The latest package of decisions suggests that EPFO is trying to balance two objectives at once: giving members greater freedom over their own money and preserving the discipline needed to keep retirement savings intact. If the new rules are implemented without friction, they could reshape how Indian workers think about provident fund balances, not as dead money locked away until old age, but as a flexible source of income, emergency support and long-term security.
